newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Arison to open talks on Hapoalim.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Arison to open talks on Hapoalim.

text.p: A group led by Arison Investments will begin negotiations with the Israeli government in the next several days on its bid for Bank Hapoalim, a spokesman for Arison said on Monday.
The spokesman would not confirm or deny a report in the Israeli daily Haaretz that the group would offer between $825 million and $890 million for a third of the shares in Israel's largest bank.
At that level, the offer values the bank at $2.48 billion to $2.67 billion, less than its present market capitalisation of $2.8 billion.
"What I can say is that the group does not see the bourse valuation as the value of the bank," the spokesman said. "The government is not selling the bank according to its share price."
Hapoalim shares have surged 61 percent in the past year, outpacing the 46 percent rise in the benchmark Mishtanim index.
Haaretz said the rise in Hapoalim's market valuation had raised speculation that some members of the group would drop out, but the spokesman denied there were any problems.
"Talks were held last week in New York. All members of the group were present and all took a final decision to participate in the bidding," the spokesman said.

Doron Tsur, head of research at Sahar Securities, said the market had not overvalued the bank. He has set a share price target of 9.5 shekels, which equals a market capitalisation of $3.4 billion. On Monday the shares were trading in mid-afternoon at 7.58 shekels, down 0.75 percent.

"Hapoalim is the cheapest of Israel's banks, trading at 9.5 to 10 times earnings against multiples of 12 to 15 for the other banks," Tsur said. "Hapoalim is the only one that has had double digit return on equity several years in a row."

Arison Investments is the Israeli investment vehicle of U.S.-Israeli entrepreneur Ted Arison, who founded Carnival Cruise Lines. The group includes Claridge Israel, the investment company controlled by Canadian Charles Bronfman; U.S. investor Michael Steinhardt and his partner Shlomo Topor; Israel's Dankner Group; U.S. investment fund Hyperion; and U.S. insurance businessman Len Abramson.
A second group bidding for Hapoalim is led by U.S. banker Jeffrey Keil and Israeli businessman Eliezer Fishman.

The Israeli government controls 78 percent of Hapoalim with the rest traded on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. It plans to sell a controlling 25 to 69.3 percent of the bank through a tender, which it hopes to complete by August.
